summary: The note is a market wrap on the ASX's expected fall after Wall Street's September slump deepened, with the S&P 500 down 5.2 per cent for the month as the realisation sets in that interest rates will stay high. It covers Betashares' deal to buy Bendigo and Adelaide Bank's super business, Star Entertainment's capital raising and record-low share price, and sector moves on the local market. It also covers Wall Street's worries (bond yields, a possible US government shutdown, oil, the autoworkers' strike, student-loan repayments, the Amazon antitrust suit, Evergrande) and a Senate quote on Alan Joyce.
one_line: ASX set to drop as Wall Street's September slump deepens on high-rate fears, with Betashares buying Bendigo's super arm and Star Entertainment hitting a record low.
key_facts: Betashares, which manages $30 billion in funds, agreed to acquire Bendigo and Adelaide Bank's superannuation business, its first venture into superannuation; Bendigo shares rose 0.6 per cent.

Star Entertainment Group shares hit an all-time low of 60¢ after it raised $565 million, closing 16 per cent weaker at 63¢; Star raised $800 million in February and hopes to raise $750 million at 60¢ a share.

REITs (up 0.4 per cent) were the strongest ASX sector, with Dexus up 2.8 per cent and Goodman up 0.5 per cent; information technology (down 1.1 per cent) was the weakest, with WiseTech down 1.4 per cent.

Gold miners Newcrest (down 2.1 per cent) and Evolution (down 3.5 per cent) fell after the spot gold price dropped 0.9 per cent overnight; CSL shed 1.4 per cent, IAG fell 2.6 per cent and Suncorp 2 per cent.

Novus Capital's Gary Glover said Australian markets 'held on pretty well' given the damage overnight in the US, and described the market as volatile but range-bound, like past high-inflation periods in the 1940s and 1970s.
On Tuesday the S&P 500 fell 1.5 per cent for its fifth loss in six days, the Dow dropped 1.1 per cent and the Nasdaq composite lost 1.6 per cent, returning stocks to June levels.
The S&P 500 is down 5.2 per cent in September, on track to be the worst month of the year, as investors accept the Federal Reserve will keep rates high for a long time.
The 10-year Treasury yield edged up to 4.55 per cent from 4.54 per cent, near its highest since 2007, up from about 3.5 per cent in May and 0.5 per cent about three years ago.

RBC's Lori Calvasina found that before the seven shutdowns lasting 10 days or more since the 1970s, the S&P 500 fell about 10 per cent on average over three months, but fell only 0.3 per cent on average during them.

Amazon fell 4 per cent after the Federal Trade Commission and 17 state attorneys general filed an antitrust lawsuit accusing it of inflating prices, overcharging sellers and stifling competition; Apple fell 2.3 per cent and Microsoft 1.7 per cent.
Benchmark US crude rose 71¢ to $US90.39 a barrel and Brent rose 67¢ to $US93.96; France's CAC 40 fell 0.7 per cent and Germany's DAX 1 per cent.

Senator Bridget McKenzie said Senate committees cannot enforce summonses on overseas witnesses, as former Qantas boss Alan Joyce declined to front the select committee on the rejection of extra Qatar Airways flights, citing 'personal commitments'.
